summary: This standards-track memo defines the MIB objects for managing UDP implementations through SNMP, independent of IP version. It obsoletes earlier UDP MIB definitions.

plainLanguage.summary: This defines the gauges that tell a network manager how a computer is using UDP, a simple way of sending messages.

questions: how to monitor udp with snmp
how to list udp endpoints with snmp
what replaced the ipv6 udp mib
subtitle: The standard set of SNMP objects for counting UDP traffic and listing the UDP endpoints on a machine, for both IPv4 and IPv6.

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to ask a machine how much UDP traffic it handles and which UDP endpoints are open. The older UDP MIBs covered only IPv4 and could not describe connected endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: The UDP-MIB defines a group of scalar counters and a udpEndpointTable that works for any IP version, lists listening and connected endpoints, and names the operating system process behind each one.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2013 and RFC 2454, deprecates the IPv4-only udpTable, and adds 64-bit counters for fast networks.

facts.label: High-capacity threshold
facts.value: More than 1 million datagrams per second

today: RFC 4113 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2013 and RFC 2454, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the UDP MIB Is
sections.content:
A Management Information Base (MIB) is a virtual information store of managed objects. Its objects are normally read through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). RFC 4113 specifies a MIB module that follows SMIv2, the second version of that language.

The module describes managed objects for implementations of the User Datagram Protocol, as defined in RFC 768, in a way that does not depend on the IP version.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is like the instrument panel of a car. This memo says which dials the UDP part of a computer should show, so every manager can read them the same way.

sections.title: What the Module Contains
sections.content:
The module has one table and a group of scalars. The udp group of scalars reports parameters and statistics of a UDP protocol engine. Two scalars, udpHCInDatagrams and udpHCOutDatagrams, were added since RFC 2013 to give high-capacity counters for fast networks.

The udpEndpointTable gives status information for all UDP endpoints handled by a UDP protocol engine. It covers strictly listening endpoints, as the historical udpTable did, and also "connected" endpoints, which only accept packets from a given remote system. Addresses and ports in this table use the InetAddressType, InetAddress and InetPortNumber textual conventions from RFC 4001.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two parts: a few counters that count messages, and a list of all the mailboxes a program has opened. The list can say whether a mailbox takes mail from anyone or only from one sender.

sections.title: The Counters
sections.content:
Four 32-bit counters sit in the udp group. udpInDatagrams is the total number of UDP datagrams delivered to UDP users. udpNoPorts counts received datagrams for which there was no application at the destination port. udpInErrors counts received datagrams that could not be delivered for any other reason. udpOutDatagrams is the total sent from this entity.

The two 64-bit counters, udpHCInDatagrams and udpHCOutDatagrams, count the same in and out totals for devices that can receive or transmit more than 1 million UDP datagrams per second. All counters can show discontinuities at re-initialization of the management system and at other times indicated by discontinuities in sysUpTime.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters are like tally clickers at a door: one for mail delivered, one for mail with no mailbox, one for mail that broke, and one for mail sent out. Fast computers get bigger clickers so they do not roll over.

sections.title: The Endpoint Table
sections.content:
Each row of udpEndpointTable is one UDP endpoint. The row is indexed by local address type, local address, local port, remote address type, remote address, remote port and an udpEndpointInstance number. The instance distinguishes several processes 'connected' to the same endpoint, for example when a BSD sockets system uses the SO_REUSEADDR and SO_REUSEPORT options.

The address type is the one used for the communication, whatever the application's abstraction. An application using IPv6 sockets to talk between ::ffff:10.0.0.1 and ::ffff:10.0.0.2 is recorded as IPv4. A listening application appears in one of three ways, shown in the table below. When the remote side is a wildcard, the remote address type is unknown(0), the remote address is a zero-length octet string and the remote port is 0.

The last column, udpEndpointProcess, holds the system's process ID for the endpoint, or zero if there is none. It is expected to match hrSWRunIndex or sysApplElmtRunIndex for some row, which lets managers tie UDP endpoints to operating system processes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row is one open mailbox. It says which address and number the mailbox has, whether it only takes mail from one friend, and which program owns it.

sections.title: Relationship to Older MIBs
sections.content:
UDP objects started in the RFC1213-MIB (RFC 1213) and were later copied into their own module in RFC 2013. The udpTable from those versions is deprecated for two reasons: it supports only IPv4, and it cannot describe 'connected' UDP endpoints, which tend to behave and be managed differently from listening ones.

The IPV6-UDP-MIB of RFC 2454 has been moved to Historic, because separate IP-version-specific tables are no longer the approach and implementing RFC 2454 is not suggested. Since scoped addresses are now carried as IPv4z and IPv6z address types, the interface index no longer has to appear in the table index. Agents are still encouraged to implement the deprecated IPv4 objects to interoperate with the deployed base of managers.
sections.plainLanguage: The old list only knew about the old kind of addresses and could not say who a mailbox talks to. The new list handles both kinds of addresses, so the old ones are put on the shelf.

sections.title: Compliance Rules
sections.content:
The current compliance statement, udpMIBCompliance2, makes udpBaseGroup and udpEndpointGroup mandatory. The group udpHCGroup is mandatory for systems capable of receiving or transmitting more than 1 million UDP datagrams per second, because at that rate a Counter32 wraps in just over an hour.

For the endpoint table indexes, support for the dns(5) address type is not required. Support is only required for zero-length octet strings and for scoped and unscoped IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. The old udpMIBCompliance and udpGroup are deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say which dials every computer must have. Only very fast computers need the extra big counters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, so correct implementations cannot be altered through SNMP SET operations. Readable objects can still be sensitive. The indexes of the endpoint table and udpTable reveal which ports are open, which tells an attacker what is likely to succeed without running a port scanner.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The list shows which doors are open on a computer, which is useful to a burglar too. So only trusted people should be allowed to read it.
